A harsh sound from the throat, like the “ch” in Scottish “loch”: Tochter, acht, Buch.
A soft sound, like a whispered “h” at the start of “huge”, with your tongue close to the roof of your mouth: ich, Mädchen, Milch.
“w” is read “v” (wer = “vair”), and “v” is usually read “f” (Vater = “FAH-ter”, vier = “feer”).
At the end of a word, “-er” is read like a short, open “uh” (as in British English, without the “r”): Vater ≈ “FAH-tuh”, Bruder ≈ “BROO-duh”.

Age is NOT said with “haben”! As in English, you say it with SEIN: “Ich bin 27 Jahre alt” (I am 27 years old). “Ich habe 27 Jahre” is a typical mistake of speakers of languages like Romanian or Spanish (“I have 27 years”) — as an English speaker you have it easy here.
German has three genders (masculine, feminine, neuter), while English nouns have none. The definite article comes BEFORE the noun:

The gender doesn't always follow the meaning: das Mädchen (the girl) is neuter, die Katze (the cat) is feminine, der Hund (the dog) masculine. Learn EVERY noun with its article, as if it were a single word: “der Hund”, not just “Hund”.
A few clues: words ending in -chen (das Mädchen, das Brötchen) are always neuter; those in -in (die Lehrerin) and -ung (die Wohnung) are always feminine.
German plurals follow several patterns. The plural article is always “die”. What changes is the ending and sometimes the vowel (with an Umlaut):
Practical rule: learn the plural together with the article: der Bruder, die Brüder. Dictionaries write “Bruder, der, -¨” or “Kind, das, -er”.
Watch out for the shortened forms: sechzehn (not “sechszehn”) and siebzehn (not “siebenzehn”).
Above 20, German says the units BEFORE the tens, with “und”: 21 = einundzwanzig (one-and-twenty), 27 = siebenundzwanzig, 29 = neunundzwanzig. You'll practise them in chapter 4.
So that it isn't confused with “drei” on the phone, “zwei” is often said as “zwo”.
“Das ist…” introduces someone or something, whatever the gender or number: “Das ist mein Vater.” “Das ist meine Mutter.” “Das sind meine Eltern.” (in the plural: das sind).
The same goes for “dein / deine” (your): “Ist das dein Bruder?”
